query: Earlier empirical-potential and first-principles studies primarily targeted phase-transition temperature, while other fusion properties remain difficult because they require free energies on both sides of the transition with vibrational entropy, anharmonicity, and electron–vibration coupling retained. Explicit ab initio free-energy evaluation is highly accurate but depends on costly molecular dynamics. TOR-TILD increased throughput for elemental and binary systems, yet slows substantially for multicomponent high-entropy systems. Under the constraint that the free energies of both solid and fluid states and the relevant entropy terms remain faithful, what single testable methodological hypothesis could substantially reduce the cost of obtaining fusion and high-temperature thermodynamic properties? State the proposed intervention and why it should work, predict its speed and fidelity relative to explicit ab initio molecular-dynamics workflows and TOR-TILD, define composition and temperature boundaries, cite supporting evidence from prior elemental or binary results, and specify a decisive benchmark of phase free energies and derived observables that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: A carefully trained machine-learning (ML) interatomic potential, using a limited set of ab initio molecular-dynamics reference data for both solid and fluid states, can faithfully reproduce free energies and derived properties for multicomponent systems at a fraction of the computational cost of explicit ab initio MD or TOR-TILD.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy systems spanning solid and fully molten phases at relevant compositions.
generation.intervention: Adopt a minimally sampled ab initio MD reference scheme to train flexible ML interatomic potentials targeting free energy calculations in both solid and liquid regimes.
generation.conditions: Simulations performed over a range of compositions representative of multicomponent alloys, for temperatures covering ambient to near the melting point (up to ~80% of the compound’s absolute melting temperature).
generation.structural_mediator: ML-generated interatomic potentials capturing short- and long-range ordering in both the crystalline and liquid states.
generation.mechanism: ML potentials emulate the full quantum-mechanical energy landscapes by interpolating from a sparse but carefully selected ab initio MD training set, preserving key energetic, entropic, and anharmonic contributions needed to compute free energies efficiently.
generation.predicted_outcome: Accurate prediction of fusion enthalpies and melting points, as well as realistic high-temperature thermodynamic properties (e.g., free energies), at least one order of magnitude lower computational cost than traditional ab initio MD or TOR-TILD.
generation.baseline: Full ab initio molecular-dynamics-based free-energy evaluations and existing TOR-TILD method results for binary or ternary alloys at comparable temperature and composition ranges.
generation.boundary: Method performance is tested for systems with 3–5 components and for temperatures extending up to ~80% of the melting point; extrapolation to extreme compositions or higher temperatures remains unproven.
generation.uncertainty: The required training data coverage for more complex high-entropy compositions is not fully established, and performance may degrade if local chemical environments deviate significantly from the reference set.

falsification_experiment.design: Select a representative high-entropy alloy composition with known melting behavior. Perform free-energy calculations for solid and liquid phases using (1) ab initio MD, (2) the proposed ML potential, and (3) TOR-TILD. Compare predicted fusion properties and computational costs.
measurements: Measured free energies (solid/liquid) from each method
Derived melting transition (fusion enthalpy, entropy, temperature)
Computational cost (CPU/GPU hours) and memory usage
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the ML-based method’s predicted free energies or melting properties deviate beyond acceptable uncertainty from ab initio or measured data, or if the computational speed is not significantly improved over ab initio MD or TOR-TILD, then the hypothesis is falsified.
